newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Hijacker takes Russian bus passengers hostage.
newsitem.headline: Hijacker takes Russian bus passengers hostage.

text.p: An man with an assault rifle and a hand grenade seized about 30 hostages aboard a bus on Monday in the southern Russian region of Dagestan, which borders Chechnya, officials said.

A spokesman for the regional interior ministry told Reuters by telephone that the unidentified man had been among passengers on a regular bus heading for the town of Kizlyar when he forced the driver to turn around and stop some 10 km (seven miles) outside Dagestani capital Makhachkala.

The head of the nearby airport police was conducting negotiations with the man, who had demanded a helicopter. Itar-Tass news agency quoted a Dagestani interior ministry official as saying he also wanted $100,000.
The hijacker had released two women and four children but was still believed to be holding some two dozen people, it said.
Officials in Dagestan and at the Russian Emergencies Ministry in Moscow said they had no information on who the man was, where he wanted to go or whether he might also have accomplices on board.

Such hijackings have not been uncommon in Russia's turbulent North Caucasus. Many have involved Chechens fighting for independence for their mainly Moslem region but others have been staged for ransom or unplanned responses to police searches.

Last September a man armed with a grenade hijacked a bus in Makhachkala and demanded a helicopter. He fled by car after freeing them and taking a local politician along as security and was later reported to have crossed into Chechnya on foot.
There were two major and bloody hostage-takings just beyond Chechnya's borders during the December 1994 to August 1996 war, one of them at Kizlyar in January 1996.

In 1994, Chechen bandits mounted a series of bus hijackings for ransom across the North Caucausus. Those were cited by the Russian authorities as a reason for launching their military campaign against the secessionist rebel government in Chechnya.
